# dsh-ai-model-hub
A modular local AI model ecosystem for **DeepSeek Harness (DSH)**.

DSH is the agent — it reasons, plans, calls tools, and orchestrates workflows.
It is **not** the mod

el runtime. The specialised models (text, image, 3D, audio,
video) are external and local, reached t

hrough a capability interface. DSH never
learns how to launch Stable Diffusion, which Python file st

arts a mesh generator,
or how a given engine manages its process. It only asks:
> **What capabilities are available?**
Everything below that question is this project's job.

### Why the package ships compiled JavaScript

The plugin's sources are TypeScript, and Node runs them directly through type
stripping while you wo

rk in a checkout. It refuses to do that inside
`node_modules`:
[代码示例省略，未执行]

A package installed by name — from GitHub, from a registry — lands *inside* the
profile's `node_modu

les`, so a `.ts` entry there could never be imported. That is
the entire reason this repository comm

its `lib/`: `lib/` is the same sources
compiled to JavaScript, and the package's entry points (`main

`, `exports`) point
at it, so `dsh plugin add` needs no build step on your machine.

`lib/` is generated, never edited: `npm run build` regenerates it from `src/` and
`dsh-plugin/`. The

one setting that makes it work is
`rewriteRelativeImportExtensions`, so the emitted JavaScript impo

rts `./x.js`
where the source said `./x.ts`.

### What the agent can then do
| Ask the agent | Tool it calls |

| "What AI models can you run?" | `list_models` |
| "What can this machine actually do?" | `list_cap

abilities` |
| "Create a futuristic city image." | `invoke_model` (`text_to_image`) → router picks t

he model |
| "Now make a 3D model from that image." | `invoke_model` (`image_to_3d`), chaining the a

rtifact id |
| "Why did it pick that model?" | `explain_routing` — read-only |
| "Is the image model

running?" | `get_model_status`, `check_model_health` |
| "Start / stop the image model." | `start_m
odel`, `stop_model` |
The agent never names an engine, a command, or a path. That is the whole design.
### A settings page for what is on this machine

The agent is not the only one who needs to know where the engines are. The plugin
also adds a **Loca

l models** section to the DSH settings, which answers the question
a user actually has: which engine

s are on this PC, where is each one installed,
is it running, and what is inside it.
| Row | Where it comes from |
| Verified installation | Engine markers or executables in configured/well-known locations; a config

ured `cwd` alone is not proof |
| Configured paths | Catalog launch paths, displayed separately from

verified installation paths |
| Listens on / availability | Independent bounded endpoint checks on

both **Scan** and **Refresh** |
| Hub can start it | The descriptor's `startable`, after the deploym

ent's `allowProcessLaunch` |
| Catalog models / capabilities | The same live hub the tools read, so
the page cannot disagree with behaviour |

**Scan** is the page's main action, and it produces one list of two kinds of
thing, each row labelle

thing, each row labelled with what it is:
| Kind | What it is | Where it comes from |
| **Ollama Model** | An observed or catalog-known model | Live `/api/tags`, offline loopback-host ma

nifests (`OLLAMA_MODELS` or `~/.ollama/models`), active catalog, or last-good observations |
| **Com
fyUI Workflow** | One complete workflow or an explained unreadable entry | Saved `/userdata` workflo
ws, verified installation's workflow store, configured directories, and active catalog inline/pinned
installation's workflow store, configured directories, and active catalog inline/pinned workflows |

A ComfyUI workflow is the smallest thing the list exposes. Its checkpoints,
LoRAs, VAEs, text encode

rs, ControlNets and individual nodes are **not** listed —
they are the workflow's own business, whic

h is why changing what a workflow loads
never changes anything an agent or a user has to know.

The two halves are discovered independently, so an Ollama instance that is down
cannot hide the work

flows and a ComfyUI that is down cannot hide the models; each
source reports its own status. Scannin

g twice refreshes the list rather than
growing it, because every entry's id comes from its source lo

refreshes the list rather than
growing it, because every entry's id comes from its source location.

### Capability priorities: order and enablement you own

Open **Settings → Local models**, then use the **Edit priorities** button at the
top left or the **P

riorities** tab. The **Inventory** tab stays mounted alongside
the editor, so switching views or res
canning does not discard an unsaved draft.

The editor uses responsive cards, human-readable capability names, provider
search, and **All / With

options / Enabled** filters. Search matches capabilities
and their providers; it keeps each matchin

g capability's full ordered list visible
so filtering never changes the meaning of a rank. Technical

status and the policy
file are available in expandable details, and **Save / Cancel** stay reachabl

e in
a sticky action bar. Light and dark colors follow the host theme.

Each capability contains every option that genuinely declares it — local models,
ComfyUI workflows,

and subscription backends in the *same* list, because to the hub
they are the same kind of thing: a
way to serve a capability.

On hosts that only report effective enablement while globally disabled, individual
editing is paused

rather than guessing at saved permissions. Enable and save the

## Requirements

- **Node ≥ 22.6** — the hub *sources* run directly through Node's type stripping
while you work in a

checkout. The installed package loads the compiled `lib/`
instead, because Node refuses to strip ty

forwards to it.
- **No runtime dependencies.** The hub is dependency-free by design: a plugin
whose

`node_modules` must resolve inside a DSH profile is a plugin that breaks
on the next release. The DS

H packages it imports are peers, supplied by the
profile that loads it.
